name: Markdown parser error
description:
1. Diagnosed that `<file_change>` block boundaries were being broken by fenced code blocks inside the file body, causing files to be truncated or the rest of the message to be swallowed.
2. First fix: made `parseFileChangeBlock` fence-aware and made tag matching indentation-strict; added regression tests for envelope examples, trailing spaces, CRLF, and long fences.
3. You then proposed a counter instead of a flag for nesting — applied a depth counter for `<file_change>` tags inside `<file_change>`, since open/close tags are unambiguous.
4. Final fix after the "ends three lines after a ```" bug: `<file_change>` blocks now ignore all fences entirely, and fenced blocks use a typed counter (`createFenceTracker`/`trackFence`) shared by `markdownParser`, `codeBlockExtractor` and `DocumentSummary.vue`.
5. Result: no flags left anywhere, deterministic block bounds, and 14 dependency-free regression tests runnable via `node tests/fileChangeParser.test.mjs`.

messages.content: Parsing code blocks is failing with `file_change` instructions. The file inside is complex and has many code blocks examples. Is it possible that parser is mixing closing fences with closing file_change?

I'll investigate the parser that handles `file_change` blocks.## 1. Verdict

**Yes — your hypothesis is correct, but the mixing happens in the *opposite* direction than you'd expect.**

It is not that a closing fence is being mistaken for `</file_change>`. It's that **`</file_change>` detection ignores fence state**, so a closing marker that belongs to a *fenced example inside the file body* is taken as the end of the envelope. Once the envelope ends too early, the remaining lines — including every fence of the example — are re-parsed as top-level markdown. From that point on, fence parity is broken for the rest of the message, which is why "a complex file with many code block examples" is exactly the trigger.

## 2. Evidence (current code on disk)

`src/utils/markdownParser.js` → `parseFileChangeBlock()`:

```js
let endIndex = lines.length
for (let i = startIndex + 1; i < lines.length; i++) {
  if (isFileChangeCloseTag(lines[i])) {   // ← no fence awareness at all
    endIndex = i
    break
  }
}
```

and the tag matchers normalize with `.trim()`:

```js
const FILE_CHANGE_OPEN_REGEX  = /^<file_change\s/i          // tested on line.trim()
const FILE_CHANGE_CLOSE_REGEX = /^<\/?file_change\s*\/?>\s*$/i // tested on line.trim()
```

Same pattern in `src/utils/codeBlockExtractor.js` → `readFileChangeBlock()` / `isFileChangeOpenTag()`.

## 3. The two failure modes

### A) Envelope example inside the file body hijacks the boundary (primary suspect)

A file that *documents* the envelope (very likely for a doc containing "many code block examples"):

```text
<file_change path="docs/protocol.md" language="markdown" change_type="update" encoding="text">
# Protocol

Example of a correct block:

```xml
<file_change path="a.md" language="markdown" change_type="new" encoding="text">
body
<file_change/>
```

End of document.
<file_change/>
```

What the parser does:

| line | current behaviour |
|---|---|
| inner `<file_change ...>` | matches `^<file_change\s` → **starts a new envelope** |
| inner `<file_change/>` | `isFileChangeCloseTag` → **closes it** (endIndex) |
| `` ``` `` | re-parsed at top level → opens a legacy fence |
| `End of document.` | swallowed as code |
| real `<file_change/>` | no longer a marker (only 1 match consumed) |
| next block of the message | now parsed *inside* a dangling fence |

Result: truncated file, `End of document.` rendered as a code block, subsequent `<file_change>` blocks lose their boundaries. That is literally "closing fences mixed with closing file_change".

Two aggravating details:
- `.trim()` on the open tag means an **indented** example in prose (`    <file_change path="x">`) also starts a real envelope.
- `.trim()` on the close tag means an **indented** `</file_change>` example closes the real block.

### B) Legacy fence scanner swallows the rest of the message

`src/utils/codeBlockExtractor.js` (used by `$service.chat.extractCodeBlocksFromMessage` → Files view, Review view, bulk-save, "Files" button):

```js
while (i < lines.length && lines[i] !== '```') {   // exact string match
```

This never closes on `` ``` `` + trailing spaces, on `` ``` `` + `\r` (CRLF content), on ```` ```` ```` (4+ backticks), or on a `~~~` closer. The loop then runs to EOF, consuming **every following `<file_change>` envelope**. Same class of defect in `DocumentSummary.vue` (`line === '```'`) and `Markdown.vue` (`lines[i].trim() === '```'`).

## 4. Root cause in one sentence

> The body of a `<file_change>` is verbatim, so you cannot decide whether `</file_change>` is the real closer without counting the fences inside that body — and the current scanner reads the body with fences disabled.

That makes closing-fence tracking and closing-marker detection **one problem, not two**. The contract (`<file_change …>` at column 0, closer at column 0) is only decidable with fence state.

## 5. Proposed fix (not applied)

One shared, fence-aware envelope scanner; every consumer (`markdownParser`, `codeBlockExtractor`, `DocumentSummary`) uses it.

**`src/utils/markdownParser.js`** — near `parseFileChangeBlock`:

```js
// Tags are only recognised at column 0 (contract); tolerates trailing \r/space
const FILE_CHANGE_OPEN_REGEX  = /^<file_change\s/i
const FILE_CHANGE_CLOSE_REGEX = /^<\/?file_change\s*\/?>\s*$/i

function parseFileChangeBlock(lines, startIndex, getRendererFn = getRenderer) {
  const attrs = parseFileChangeAttributes(lines[startIndex])

  let endIndex = lines.length
  let fence = null      // fence opened inside the body
  let nestDepth = 0     // named fences nested inside `fence`

  for (let i = startIndex + 1; i < lines.length; i++) {
    const line = lines[i]

    // The closer only counts at depth 0: fences in the body are verbatim and
    // may legitimately contain the tag as an example.
    if (!fence && isFileChangeCloseTag(line)) { endIndex = i; break }

    const lineFence = getFence(line)
    if (!lineFence) continue

    if (!fence) { fence = lineFence; nestDepth = 0; continue }

    if (isClosingFence(line, fence)) {
      if (nestDepth > 0) nestDepth--
      else fence = null
      continue
    }
    if (lineFence.info && lineFence.info.trim()) nestDepth++
  }
  ...
}
```

and drop the `.trim()` from both matchers:

```js
function isFileChangeOpenTag(line) {
  return !!line && FILE_CHANGE_OPEN_REGEX.test(line)       // was: line.trim()
}
function isFileChangeCloseTag(line) {
  return !!line && FILE_CHANGE_CLOSE_REGEX.test(line)      // was: line.trim()
}
```

**`src/utils/codeBlockExtractor.js`** — replace the legacy inner loop and reuse the shared helpers:

```js
import { getFence, isClosingFence, parseFileChangeBlock, getFileChangeOpenTag } from './markdownParser'

// inside extractCodeBlocks(), before the legacy branch:
let fence = null, nestDepth = 0

if (!fence && getFileChangeOpenTag(line)) {
  const { block, endIndex } = parseFileChangeBlock(lines, i)
  if (block.filePath) codeBlocks.push(block)
  i = endIndex + 1
  continue
}
// legacy branch: collect until a *valid* closing fence for `fence`
```

**`src/components/document/DocumentSummary.vue`** — same treatment: skip envelope bodies verbatim and stop using `line === '```'`.

**Regression tests worth pinning** (the four cases that break today):

1. envelope body containing a fenced example of the envelope (nested `</file_change>`);
2. closing fence with trailing spaces;
3. CRLF content (`\r` after ` ``` `);
4. ```` ````markdown ```` wrapper containing ` ``` ` examples.

## 6. Open questions before I apply it

1. **Where did you actually see the failure** — the chat body (client, `markdownParser`), the Files/Review panel (`codeBlockExtractor`), or the *changes not being written to disk*? If it's the last one, the defect is in the **backend parser**, which is not in this workspace (`/client`); send me that file and I'll patch both sides identically.

If you confirm the client-side symptom, say the word and I'll apply the three patches above plus the four regression cases.

messages.content:
There's a case where a "file_change" has nested "file_chance" inside, it can happen as well with standard fence "```ext"
So when detecting an opening fence I'll be using a counter instead of a flag, next opnening increases, closing decreases and when reach zero is the end of the block. In this way nested fences are not treated as blocks but as part of the content.

dont you?

I'll re-read the current parser before answering, because the answer differs between the two syntaxes.## 1. Verdict

**Yes for `<file_change>` tags — a counter is not just better, it's the only correct fix for the case you describe. No for bare ```` ``` ```` fences — there a pure counter is undecidable and the code already uses a counter where it can.**

Two different syntaxes, two different disambiguation problems:

| Syntax | Can you tell open from close? | Right tool |
|---|---|---|
| `<file_change path=…>` vs `<file_change/>` | **Yes, unambiguously** (attributes vs leading `/`) | **Counter** — nothing else needed |
| ```` ``` ```` vs ```` ``` ```` | **No** — same token both ways | Counter **+** open/close decision rule |

That distinction is why your instinct is right for the envelope and can't be applied verbatim to fences.

## 2. What is actually broken today

`parseFileChangeBlock()` (current code on disk) tracks **fences** but never tracks **nested open tags**:

```js
for (let i = startIndex + 1; i < lines.length; i++) {
  if (isFileChangeCloseTag(line) && (!fenceStack.length || !isFenceClosedLater(...))) { endIndex = i; break }
  // ... only getFence/isClosingFence below — a nested `<file_change ...>` is ignored
}
```

So an **unfenced** nested envelope — a model emitting a real nested block, not a fenced example:

```text
<file_change path="a.md" ...>
intro
<file_change path="b.md" ...>
inner
<file_change/>
outer tail
<file_change/>
```

…closes at the inner `<file_change/>` and `outer tail` is lost. The fence stack from the previous turn only rescues the case where the example is wrapped in ```` ``` ````. Your case isn't rescued at all. A depth counter closes exactly this gap, and it also makes the previous `isFenceClosedLater()` guard redundant for the *fenced-documenting-the-envelope* scenario, because balanced nesting is self-cancelling: inner open `+1`, inner close `−1`, real close reaches `0`.

## 3. Why a pure counter fails for ```` ``` ````

A fence line is ambiguous. On ```` ``` ```` you must decide *before* you can increment or decrement:

- Rule "bare fence always closes when depth > 0" → a ```` ```markdown ```` body containing a **bare** ```` ```…``` ```` pair closes the outer block at the first bare fence. This is precisely what `isNestedAnonymousFence()` (`countClosingFencesAhead >= 2`) exists to prevent.
- So the decision rule has to be *"has an info string → open; no info string → close if it matches char/length"*, and that is what `parseBlocks()` already does:

```js
if (isClosingFence(line, currentFence)) {
  if (nestDepth > 0) { nestDepth--; currentContent.push(line) }   // ← your counter
  else { addBlock(true); inCodeBlock = false }
} else {
  if (fence.info && fence.info.trim()) nestDepth++                 // ← your counter
  currentContent.push(line)
}
```

`nestDepth` **is** the counter you're describing, applied to the only case where it's decidable. So for fences: nothing to change (except one edge, see §5.3).

## 4. Proposed change (hybrid, not applied)

**Rule: fences *mask* tags; tags *nest*.** Inside a fence, tag lines are verbatim and must not touch the depth (that's how an unbalanced sample stays harmless). Outside a fence, open/close is unambiguous, so the counter runs.

```js
// src/utils/markdownParser.js → parseFileChangeBlock()
let depth = 1                // the envelope we are parsing
let fenceStack = []          // verbatim mask
let lastCloseIndex = null    // safety valve for unbalanced bodies

for (let i = startIndex + 1; i < lines.length; i++) {
  const line = lines[i]
  const inFence = fenceStack.length > 0

  if (!inFence && getFileChangeOpenTag(line)) {
    depth++
    continue
  }

  if (!inFence && isFileChangeCloseTag(line)) {
    depth--
    lastCloseIndex = i
    if (depth === 0) { endIndex = i; break }
    continue
  }

  const lineFence = getFence(line)
  if (!lineFence) continue
  if (!inFence) { fenceStack = [lineFence]; continue }
  if (isClosingFence(line, fenceStack[fenceStack.length - 1])) fenceStack.pop()
  else if (lineFence.info) fenceStack.push(lineFence)
}

// Unbalanced body (a bare example of the opening tag with no closer):
// fall back to the last closer seen so one stray tag can never swallow
// the rest of the message.
if (depth > 0 && lastCloseIndex !== null) endIndex = lastCloseIndex
```

`isInsideCodeFence()` gets the same `fileChangeDepth` counter (it currently only flips a boolean, so a nested envelope makes it exit early and headings inside the rest of the outer body get promoted to chapters).

`codeBlockExtractor` and `DocumentSummary` need **no change** — they delegate to `parseFileChangeBlock()`.

## 5. Three details worth your decision
